Operator: Good day, and welcome to the VeriStream Communications Fourth Quarter 2023 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. As a reminder, please refrain from using your telephone keypad during the presentation. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera: Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and welcome to VeriStream Communications' Fourth Quarter 2023 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me on the call today are Sarah Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Chen, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Patel, Chief Network Officer; David Kim, Chief Commercial Officer; Elena Vasquez, Chief Technology Officer; and other members of our leadership team.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements. These statements are based on management's current expectations and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more complete discussion of these risks.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. We're very pleased with our performance in the fourth quarter, driven by strong execution and a favorable market environment. We are focused on delivering long-term sustainable growth.

Our achievements include robust free cash flow generation that exceeded expectations, supporting strategic returns to shareholders. We are also seeing substantial growth from our content and media initiatives, with impressive subscriber gains and profitability improvements. Further, we are concentrating on disciplined network investments in 5G deployment, which are yielding coverage expansions and efficiency gains. Additionally, our churn rates have trended downward impressively across segments. We are also improving our debt profile and leverage ratios through proactive management. We are strategically investing in subscriber additions, particularly in residential and business segments. Finally, our dividend sustainability remains rock-solid, backed by predictable cash flows.

Michael Chen: Thank you, Sarah. Moving to the financials, our revenue for the quarter was $28.4 billion, representing a 4.2% year-over-year increase. Adjusted EBITDA was $10.2 billion, resulting in a margin of 36%, expanding 120 basis points. We continue to manage our expenses prudently and are optimizing our capital allocation. Capital expenditures were $7.5 billion for the full year, primarily focused on expanding our 5G network and fiber infrastructure.

Good afternoon, everyone—though it's morning here, thank you for joining our Q4 and full-year 2023 earnings call for VeriStream Communications. As your CFO, I'm pleased to dive into our free cash flow performance, which remains a cornerstone of our financial strength in this dynamic telecom and media landscape. For the quarter, we generated $2.8 billion in free cash flow, up 20% year-over-year and 12% sequentially from Q3. This brings our full-year 2023 free cash flow to a robust $11.2 billion, exceeding our initial guidance midpoint by $400 million and marking our strongest annual figure since the 2021 spectrum normalization post-C-band auction.

Let me break down the generation drivers. Starting with the top line, our adjusted EBITDA grew 8% year-over-year to $4.9 billion in Q4, fueled by a 4% rise in wireless service revenues to $15.2 billion, driven by postpaid ARPU expansion of 3.2% to $58.40—primarily from premium 5G Unlimited plans and our bundling of VeriStream+ streaming service, which now has 28 million subscribers, up 15% YoY. Broadband revenues in our fixed-line segment hit $6.1 billion, with DOCSIS 3.1 upgrades enabling 42% household penetration of gigabit speeds, supporting a 2% ARPU lift to $72 monthly.

On the cash conversion side, operating cash flow reached $4.2 billion in Q4, benefiting from disciplined working capital management—days sales outstanding improved by 2 days to 42, thanks to streamlined B2B invoicing with enterprise clients like our hyperscaler partners. The real story, however, is capex discipline. We deployed $7.5 billion in full-year capital expenditures, or 14.2% of revenues, down 150 basis points YoY as a percentage of sales. This reflects the maturation of our 5G Standalone core network rollout, where we've now lit up mid-band C-band spectrum across 85% of our top 100 metro markets, achieving spectral efficiency gains of 25% via massive MIMO and beamforming optimizations. In fixed broadband, our FTTH passings grew 18% to 22 million homes, but at a unit cost per foot down 12% through vendor consolidation with Nokia and CommScope, and increased adoption of Open RAN architectures in greenfield deployments—now 35% of new sites.

Regionally, this FCF strength was broad-based. In North America, which accounts for 78% of our wireless subs, we saw $2.1 billion of Q4 FCF, propelled by sub-1% postpaid churn at 0.92% and 5G adoption exceeding 65% of our 110 million connections. Europe, via our joint venture with Vodafone in the UK and Germany, contributed $450 million, with ARPU stabilizing post-inflation at €18 monthly amid regulatory tailwinds from the EU's Gigabit Infrastructure Act, accelerating our 10G PON pilots. In APAC, our SpectrumCo partnership in India generated $250 million, riding Jio-like subscriber adds of 4 million in Q4, though capex intensity remains higher at 18% of local revenues due to ongoing 5G NSA-to-SA migrations.

Turning to utilization—because strong FCF is only as good as how we deploy it strategically. In FY2023, we returned $7.1 billion to shareholders, or 63% of FCF: $4.2 billion in dividends at our target 45-50% payout ratio, with the quarterly dividend raised 5% to $0.68 per share, and $2.9 billion in share repurchases under our $10 billion authorization, retiring 4.2% of outstanding shares at an average price of $42. This enhances EPS accretion amid cord-cutting pressures, where traditional video subs declined 8% but were more than offset by streaming growth.

We also deleveraged by $2.4 billion, reducing net debt to $68 billion and our leverage ratio to 2.3x net debt-to-EBITDA—well within our 2.0-2.5x target band, positioning us ahead of peers like AT&T and T-Mobile in a rising rate environment. The remainder, $1.7 billion, went to high-return investments: $900 million for AWS Outposts edge computing integrations to slash content delivery latency for VeriStream+ by 40%, supporting our ad-tier launch that drove 22% ARPU uplift in streaming; and $800 million in tuck-in M&A, including the $450 million acquisition of indie studio PixelForge to bolster our FAST channel portfolio, now monetizing at $2.50 average CPM versus industry $1.80.

Strategically, this FCF profile underscores our 'Network First, Content Smart' thesis. In a world of intensifying competition—Comcast's Xfinity Mobile expansion, Charter's all-fiber push, and Disney's Hulu bundle—we're prioritizing ROI-positive capex. Our 2024 guidance calls for $11.5-$12.5 billion in FCF, with capex at $7.0-$7.5 billion, assuming 2-3% wireless ARPU growth from AI-driven personalization and continued 5G Fixed Wireless Access ramp to 5 million homes. We'll maintain 60%+ to shareholders, with opportunistic spectrum buys ahead of the FCC's 3.45 GHz auction and potential CBRS Priority Access Licenses for private networks.

Now, shifting to our commitment to shareholder returns, with a particular focus on dividend sustainability. In an industry navigating 5G capex cycles, spectrum auctions, and the ongoing shift from linear TV to streaming, our fortress-like balance sheet and predictable cash flows position us to deliver industry-leading returns while investing for growth.

First, let's reaffirm our quarterly dividend declaration. Today, our Board approved a $0.65 per share dividend, payable December 15th to shareholders of record by November 28th. This marks our 18th consecutive quarterly increase, bringing our annualized dividend to $2.60 per share—a 5% hike from last year and yielding approximately 4.8% based on yesterday's close. Over the trailing 12 months, we've returned $6.8 billion in dividends alone to our 2.6 billion shares outstanding, underscoring our 'cash flow machine' status in telecom and media.

On sustainability—investors often ask how we maintain this payout amid high capex for our nationwide 5G Standalone (SA) rollout and Open RAN trials. The answer lies in our robust free cash flow generation. Q3 FCF came in at $3.9 billion, ahead of consensus by $200 million, driven by wireless service revenue growth of 3.8% to $16.7 billion—bolstered by postpaid phone net adds of 456,000—and broadband expansions adding 312,000 fiber customers. Year-to-date FCF stands at $10.7 billion, covering our $6.8 billion TTM dividends by a healthy 1.57x multiple.

Our payout ratio remains disciplined at 52% of adjusted FCF, well below the telecom peer average of 65%—think Verizon's 54% or AT&T's post-spin 62%. This leaves ample headroom for reinvestment. For context, our dividend coverage ratio, using levered FCF, is 1.85x, up from 1.65x a year ago, thanks to our $1.2 billion in cost synergies from last year's integration of our regional MVNO acquisition, EchoMobile. We've also derisked via $4.5 billion in pension contributions this year, reducing volatility.

Looking at trends, our compound annual dividend growth rate (CAGR) over the past five years is 7.2%, outpacing inflation and matching the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats benchmark. This is no accident—it's fueled by structural tailwinds. In the U.S., our 5G mid-band spectrum holdings—totaling 3,200 MHz post-C-band auction—drive ARPU expansion to $52.40, up 2.1%, while fixed wireless access (FWA) pilots in underserved markets like the Midwest are scaling to 150,000 subs, with 40% take rates. In Europe, our Vodafone JV stake generates €2.1 billion in stable equity income, with dividend yields there at 6.2% amid lower capex intensity post-4G saturation.

Regionally, Asia-Pacific shines: Our IndiTel subsidiary grew FCF 12% YoY to $1.8 billion, supported by Jio-like pricing discipline and 5G uptake hitting 28% penetration in urban India. Latin America, however, faces headwinds from FX volatility in Brazil—where our Claro unit saw ARPU pressure from inflation—but we've hedged 85% of exposures, preserving a 1.4x FCF coverage.

Beyond dividends, total shareholder returns tell the full story. In 2023, we deployed $12.4 billion across dividends and buybacks—$6.8 billion in cash dividends and $5.6 billion repurchasing 210 million shares at an average $26.50, retiring 8% of float. This drove a 14.2% total shareholder return (TSR) YTD, outperforming the MSCI World Telecom Index's 9.8% and Comcast's 11.5%. Our $15 billion authorization has $9.2 billion remaining, with opportunistic pacing tied to our net debt-to-EBITDA of 2.3x—investment-grade territory, below T-Mobile's 2.8x.

Strategically, sustainability hinges on three pillars. One: Revenue diversification. Media now contributes 22% of EBITDA via our Peacock+ streaming bundle, which crossed 45 million paid subs—up 18% YoY—thanks to NFL Sunday Ticket integration and AI-driven content personalization reducing churn to 1.9%. This offsets cord-cutting, where linear video subs declined just 2.1% versus industry 5%. Two: Capex efficiency. We're targeting a 5G opex-to-capex pivot, with virtualized RAN cutting tower costs 15% and our Open RAN deal with Nokia/Qualcomm yielding $300 million in 2024 savings. Total capex guidance holds at $18-19 billion, or 65% of depreciation, freeing FCF. Three: M&A discipline. We're eyeing bolt-on content plays, like a potential 20% stake in a regional streamer akin to Paramount's BET, funded by asset sales—$2.3 billion from tower monetizations closed Q3.

Forward-looking, we guide to 2024 FCF of $14.5-15.0 billion, supporting 4-6% dividend growth and $4-5 billion in buybacks. Our TSR target remains 10-12% annually through the decade, leveraging 3-4% organic revenue growth from edge computing services and enterprise 5G private networks. In a world of rising rates and media disruption, VeriStream's 50-year dividend history—never cut, even through dot-com or GFC—affirms our sustainability.

Before moving on, let me provide some color on our balance sheet strength, particularly our debt levels and leverage ratios, which continue to underpin our ability to execute on our multi-year transformation strategy in the hyper-competitive telecom and media landscape.

As many of you know, the telecom and media sectors are capital-intensive by nature—think massive 5G spectrum auctions, nationwide fiber deployments, and content amortization from streaming wars. We've navigated this environment thoughtfully since our 2022 merger of legacy telecom assets with our media properties, including the acquisition of StreamCast Networks, which bolstered our direct-to-consumer DTC offerings akin to what Disney did with Hulu and ESPN+ integration.

Starting with the headline numbers: As of quarter-end, our gross debt stood at $52.4 billion, comprising $28 billion in senior unsecured notes, $15 billion in term loans from our syndicated credit facility, and $9.4 billion in secured tower revenue bonds tied to our cell site monetization with American Tower. After netting out $10.2 billion in cash and short-term investments—bolstered by $2.1 billion in Q4 free cash flow generation—our net debt is $42.2 billion.

On leverage, our trailing twelve-month Adjusted EBITDA for the period came in at $13.2 billion, reflecting 8% year-over-year growth driven by wireless subscriber net adds of 1.2 million, a 2.5% ARPU uplift from premium 5G Unlimited plans, and media ad revenue rebounding 12% amid digital video programmatic shifts. This translates to a net debt to Adjusted EBITDA ratio of 3.2x—down 55 basis points sequentially and a full 0.55 turn year-over-year. For context, this positions us comfortably within our target range of 2.8x to 3.2x, and squarely in line with peers: Verizon at 2.6x, T-Mobile at 2.9x post-sprint synergies, and Comcast at 3.1x including NBCUniversal debt.

Let me break down the drivers of this deleveraging trajectory, which we view as a core pillar of our capital allocation framework. First, robust EBITDA growth outpacing debt amortization. Our TTM EBITDA margin expanded to 42% from 39% a year ago, fueled by operational efficiencies like our Open RAN pilot deployments in 15 markets—reducing 5G capex intensity by 18% versus traditional vendors like Ericsson and Nokia—and fixed wireless access (FWA) launches hitting 750,000 subscribers, mirroring T-Mobile's playbook but with our media bundling edge via StreamCast. Regionally, North America contributed 72% of EBITDA with stable 3.1x leverage there, while EMEA saw leverage compress to 3.4x on 5G Standalone core network rollouts in the UK and Germany, where we've captured 25% market share in mid-band C-band spectrum. In Latin America, our Claro Brasil JV is a bright spot, delivering 15% EBITDA growth and pulling regional leverage down to 2.9x despite currency headwinds from the real.

Second, proactive debt management. We've refinanced $4.5 billion in near-term maturities at blended rates of 4.2% versus prior 5.8%, extending our weighted average debt maturity to 7.2 years with no major cliffs until 2027. Covenant headroom remains ample—4.1x First Lien leverage versus a 4.5x trigger—and our liquidity is $18.7 billion, including $8.5 billion undrawn revolver capacity. We also monetized $1.2 billion from non-core tower sales to Crown Castle in Q4, with more fiber dark pool divestitures planned for next year.

Third, capex peaking as a tailwind. Total capex was $2.7 billion in the quarter, or 36% of revenue, but we're guiding to a 5% sequential decline ahead as 5G coverage hits 98% in the US—on par with AT&T's milestone—and we pivot toward maintenance capex of 18-20% of revenue by 2025. This should unlock $12-14 billion in annual FCF, directing 40% to deleveraging, 30% to dividends (yielding 4.2% forward), and the balance to share repurchases and bolt-on M&A like regional MVNO tuck-ins.

Strategically, this balance sheet fortifies us for industry inflection points: the 6GHz unlicensed spectrum opening for Wi-Fi 7 and private 5G networks, where we're investing $500 million in edge computing via partnerships with AWS; converging fixed-mobile convergence (FMC) bundles to defend against cable peers like Charter; and media M&A amid consolidation, with $5 billion dry powder for content IP post the Warner-Discovery model. Risks? Persistent inflation in tower leases and potential FCC auction costs, but our pro forma leverage post any C-band repayment would still be sub-3.0x.

Looking ahead, we expect net leverage to trend toward 2.9x by year-end 2024 and 2.7x by 2025, assuming mid-single-digit EBITDA growth and steady FCF conversion. This gives us peer-leading flexibility to return capital while funding innovation.

I'll now turn to our Content and Media segment, which continues to be a cornerstone of our diversified portfolio, blending traditional pay-TV assets with high-growth streaming and digital media properties. This quarter, the segment delivered resilient performance amid ongoing industry headwinds like cord-cutting and linear TV fragmentation, while accelerating our pivot to direct-to-consumer models.

Starting with revenue: The segment generated $2.8 billion in Q4, up 7% year-over-year on an adjusted basis, or 9% excluding foreign exchange impacts. This marks our third consecutive quarter of organic growth, driven by a 15% surge in streaming revenue to $1.2 billion, which now represents 43% of total segment revenue—up from 35% a year ago. Traditional affiliate and carriage fees from our cable networks, including our stakes in premium channels akin to those from Discovery and Paramount Global partnerships, contributed $1.1 billion, flat YoY as we navigated retransmission consent renewals with major MVPDs like Charter and DirecTV. Advertising revenue came in at $450 million, down 3% due to softer linear ad demand but partially offset by a 25% ramp in connected TV (CTV) ad sales via our proprietary ad tech platform, which leverages AI-driven dynamic ad insertion similar to The Trade Desk's integrations.

On a regional basis, U.S. revenue grew 8%, fueled by bundling synergies with our broadband base—over 60% of our streaming subs are now broadband households. Internationally, APAC and EMEA added $150 million, up 12% YoY, thanks to localized content slates on our platforms, including cricket rights in India and Bundesliga streaming deals in Germany, where we've expanded via partnerships with telcos like Vodafone.

Turning to profitability: Adjusted EBITDA for the segment reached $950 million, a robust 34% margin—expanding 250 basis points YoY. This reflects operating leverage from streaming scale, where content amortization costs per subscriber fell 18% to $12.50, benefiting from our hit original series like 'Empire of Shadows' and sports anthologies rivaling Netflix's live events push. Operating income was $650 million, up 11%, after $200 million in targeted cost-outs, including rationalizing legacy linear production and shifting to cloud-based encoding with AWS and Akamai for 5G-optimized delivery. Free cash flow contribution from the segment hit $400 million, underscoring our ability to fund content investments without diluting shareholder value.

Now, subscriber metrics paint a clear picture of transformation. Total video RGUs—spanning linear pay-TV and streaming—stood at 48.2 million, down 2% YoY or 150,000 net losses quarter-over-quarter, in line with industry trends where Nielsen reports U.S. pay-TV households contracting at 4-5% annually. However, this masks strength in DTC: our flagship SVOD/AVOD streaming service, StreamHub, ended the quarter with 28.5 million paid subscribers globally, up 1.2 million net adds QoQ and 22% YoY. That's ahead of peers like Peacock's trajectory, driven by ad-supported tier adoption—now 40% of new subs at $5.99/month versus $11.99 for ad-free.

ARPU held steady at $14.20, up 2% YoY, bolstered by price increases on premium bundles (+$2 in July) and upsell features like 4K/HDR add-ons and offline downloads. Churn compressed to 1.8% monthly—our best in two years—thanks to machine learning personalization engines, which boosted engagement by 15% via recommendation algorithms akin to those powering YouTube's algorithm. Video net adds broke out as follows: +850,000 streaming, -1.0 million linear pay-TV. Regionally, U.S. streaming subs hit 22 million (77% of total), with EMEA adding 400,000 on soccer streaming pacts, while APAC grew to 3.5 million amid 5G rollout in Southeast Asia.

Key trends and technical initiatives underpinning this: We're leaning into hybrid monetization, with AVOD now 25% of streaming revenue, projecting $500 million annualized run-rate from CTV ads by year-end. Technologically, our 5G edge caching partnerships with Ericsson and Nokia have reduced latency to under 5 seconds for live sports, enhancing viewer retention by 12%. Content-wise, we've greenlit $1.5 billion in originals for FY24, focusing on unscripted formats and IP extensions from our media library, while securing NBA and NFL digital rights extensions to counter Amazon Prime Video's encroachment.

Strategically, this positions us for margin expansion to 37% next year as streaming achieves breakeven at scale—already cash positive on a standalone basis. We're prioritizing broadband-video convergence, targeting 10 million bundled households by EOY, and exploring M&A in ad tech to rival Magnite and PubMatic. Risks remain around content licensing costs, up 5% industry-wide per Deloitte, and macroeconomic ad softness, but our diversified revenue—60% recurring subscriptions—provides a buffer.

As we dive into our operational metrics, I'd like to focus on net subscriber additions by segment—residential and business—which remain a cornerstone of our growth story in this competitive landscape. For the quarter, we delivered total net subscriber additions of 425,000, marking a 15% year-over-year increase and accelerating 8% sequentially from Q3. This performance underscores our execution on fiber expansion, 5G Standalone rollout, and targeted bundling strategies amid ongoing cord-cutting pressures and enterprise digital transformation demands.

Starting with residential, which accounted for 78% of our net adds this quarter at 330,000—our strongest residential quarter since early 2022. In broadband, we added 185,000 net subscribers, driven by our aggressive Fiber-to-the-Home deployments. We've now passed 2.5 million homes with gigabit-capable fiber, up 25% YoY, with take rates hitting 42% in newly built territories—well ahead of our 35% target. This compares favorably to peers like AT&T's Fiber segment. Residential broadband churn held steady at 1.1%, below the industry average of 1.4%, thanks to our 'VeriStream Unlimited' bundle integrating 1 Gbps symmetric speeds with ad-supported streaming tiers from partners like Peacock and Paramount+.

Wireless postpaid net adds came in at 165,000, fueled by our mid-band 5G C-band expansion, now covering 85% of our top 100 markets. Family plan migrations from legacy 4G boosted this, with average revenue per user up 3.2% YoY to $52.50 on 5G device upgrade incentives. However, prepaid adds were flat at +10,000 due to softer demand in rural overlays, where we're piloting fixed wireless access as a broadband alternative—early trials in the Midwest yielded 15,000 net adds at 300 Mbps speeds.

Offsetting these gains, video net adds were -20,000, reflecting persistent cord-cutting trends, with linear TV households declining 4% QoQ. Our pivot to skinny bundles with Hulu + Live TV integrations mitigated this, stabilizing video ARPU at $45 amid competition from YouTube TV and Fubo. Regionally, Northeast markets like New York and Boston contributed 45% of residential adds, leveraging dense urban fiber passes, while Sunbelt expansions in Texas and Florida added 30%, though weather disruptions capped potential by ~5,000 adds.

Shifting to business, we achieved 95,000 net additions—a standout 28% YoY growth and 12% QoQ acceleration—highlighting our enterprise momentum in a segment growing at 2x the residential pace industry-wide.

Small and medium business led with 65,000 net adds, primarily in managed Wi-Fi and SD-WAN services. Our 'VeriStream Edge' platform, integrating Cisco Meraki hardware with our private 5G slices, resonated with retail and hospitality verticals, securing wins like 500-location rollouts with regional chains akin to Starbucks' partnerships with Verizon. SMB churn improved to 1.8% from 2.2% YoY, supported by 24/7 NOC monitoring and AI-driven anomaly detection.

Enterprise net adds totaled 30,000, concentrated in cloud interconnect and edge computing. Key wins included multi-year contracts with financial services firms in Chicago for low-latency 5G MEC at under 5ms, positioning us against Lumen's enterprise declines. We've expanded our National Ethernet backbone to 1.2 million route miles, enabling 100 Gbps services that powered 40% of these adds. Regionally, West Coast tech hubs drove 55% of enterprise growth, while Midwest manufacturing ramps—tied to Industry 4.0 initiatives—added momentum despite macroeconomic headwinds.

To put this in perspective, our blended quarterly churn rate across segments was 1.25%, down 20 basis points YoY, reflecting proactive retention via our 'VeriStream Loyalty' AI scoring engine, which flags at-risk accounts 30 days early. This has sustained gross adds at 1.1 million for the quarter.

Strategically, these results validate our 'Fiber First, 5G Everywhere' roadmap: We've accelerated FTTH capex to $1.8 billion for FY23, targeting 4 million passed locations by year-end, while our 3.45 GHz CBRS deployments unlock FWA scalability in underserved markets. Looking ahead, we expect Q1 residential net adds of 300,000-350,000 and business at 90,000-110,000, with upside from holiday 5G phone promotions and SMB holiday hiring cycles. In a market where T-Mobile's aggressive pricing pressures postpaid ARPU but boosts volume, our premium bundling and B2B focus de-risks growth.

Today, I'd also like to dive deep into our churn rate performance, a key leading indicator for our subscriber retention and long-term revenue stability here at VeriStream Communications. In the hyper-competitive telecom and media landscape—where we're battling the likes of Verizon, T-Mobile, Comcast, and streaming pure-plays such as Netflix and Disney+—managing churn is paramount to defending our 150 million+ global subscriber base across postpaid mobile, fixed broadband, and our flagship VeriStream SVOD platform. Churn directly impacts our postpaid ARPU trajectory, service margin expansion, and free cash flow generation.

Starting with the headlines for Q4: blended churn across our portfolio improved to 1.45%, down 15 basis points quarter-over-quarter and 25 basis points year-over-year. This marks our best quarterly result since the post-pandemic normalization. Drilling into segments: Postpaid Mobile Churn at 1.10%, a 10 bps QoQ improvement and 30 bps YoY decline, outperforming the industry benchmark of ~1.5%. Fixed Broadband Churn at an industry-leading 0.75%, flat QoQ but down 20 bps YoY. VeriStream SVOD Churn at 4.20%, up slightly 5 bps QoQ due to seasonal content gaps but down 40 bps YoY from enhanced personalization—for context, this trails Netflix's ~4.5-5% but beats Hulu's mid-5s.

Trend Analysis: Over the past 12 months, our churn trajectory has been decisively downward, reflecting a V-shaped recovery from the 1.85% blended peak, when supply chain disruptions and inflation first hit. YoY, postpaid mobile churn has compressed by 45 bps cumulatively, broadband by 35 bps, and SVOD by 60 bps—fueled by a 22% reduction in voluntary churn through targeted interventions. Seasonally, Q4 churn ticked up modestly from Q3's trough, aligning with family plan adjustments and promotional fatigue. Our 4-quarter rolling average is now at 1.52%, positioning us for sustained sub-1.4% territory in FY2024.

Key Drivers of Churn: Positive Tailwinds contributing ~60% to Improvement: Network Superiority from our $12 billion CapEx to 5G SA and Open RAN has slashed mobile churn by 25% in upgraded markets. Latency-sensitive customers—gamers on our esports bundle and AR/VR users—show 40% lower attrition. Content Ecosystem Synergies: Bundling VeriStream with mobile/broadband drove a 15% uplift in family plan tenure, with exclusives like our 'TeleMedia Originals' reducing SVOD churn by 35 bps YoY. Pricing Discipline: Postpaid ARPU grew 3.2% YoY to $58.40, offset by value-adds like unlimited 5G data and free Paramount+ tiers, limiting price-induced churn to under 5%.

Headwinds accounting for ~40% of Residual Churn: Competitive Intensity from T-Mobile's promotions poached ~20% of involuntary mobile disconnects. Macro Pressures drove 15% of broadband churn via service move activations. Technical Friction from legacy copper-to-fiber migrations caused a one-time 8 bps spike, now resolved.

Regional Commentary: North America (75% of Revenue): U.S. postpaid churn at 1.05% (best-in-class vs. Verizon's 1.15%). Europe (15%): Elevated at 1.75% blended, pressured by roaming regs. Emerging Markets (10%): Highest at 2.10%, but improving with 4G/5G push.

Technical Initiatives: Our AI-Powered Retention Engine on Google Cloud's Vertex AI analyzes 500+ behavioral signals to predict churn risk with 92% accuracy, proactively retaining 1.2 million subscribers YTD via personalized offers yielding 65% take rate. Proactive Network Diagnostics cut involuntary churn 30%. Loyalty Ecosystem boosted tenure by 18 months. Bundling 2.0 at 40% penetration with 50% lower churn.

Churn compression is accretive to our EBITDA guidance, adding ~$400 million in avoided revenue leakage. For FY2024, we guide blended churn to 1.30-1.40%, with upside from holiday bundling and spectrum wins enabling sub-1% mobile churn.

Lisa Patel: Thank you, Michael. I'd like to provide an update on our network performance. We've made significant strides in expanding our 5G coverage and increasing network capacity. We're also investing in advanced technologies like network slicing and edge computing to support new applications and services. Our network uptime and reliability remain high at over 99.99%. Turning now to our network investments, which remain the cornerstone of our long-term growth strategy in both telecommunications and media. We've been aggressively advancing our 5G deployment to capture surging demand for high-bandwidth, low-latency services and unlock new revenue streams in enterprise private networks, fixed wireless access, and immersive media experiences.

First, on 5G deployment progress: We're making tremendous strides across our non-standalone and standalone architectures. As of quarter-end, we've achieved 95% 5G population coverage in our top 50 metro markets, up from 82% a year ago, leveraging our mid-band C-band spectrum from the 2021 FCC auction and low-band 600 MHz for ubiquitous coverage. Nationwide, we're at 72% coverage, with a focus on densification in high-traffic urban corridors.

Key technical milestones include: Full 5G SA core rollout in 45 major cities, enabling network slicing for differentiated services supporting ultra-reliable low-latency communications for media partnerships like seamless 8K streaming trials with Disney and cloud gaming with Xbox, where latency dropped to under 10ms. Deployment of massive MIMO 64T64R radios from Nokia and Samsung across 15,000 sites, boosting spectral efficiency by 30% and handling the 5G data traffic surge—now 28% of total mobile data, up 55% YoY. Open RAN initiatives: We've virtualized 20% of our RAN in the Northeast, partnering with Mavenir and Parallel Wireless, reducing TCO by 15-20% and scaling to the West Coast next year. Fixed Wireless Access expansion: Added 450,000 5G FWA subscribers quarter-over-quarter, targeting 2 million by year-end, competing with T-Mobile's fiber-alternative and driving broadband ARPU uplift of $12 per user.

Regionally: Northeast and California at 98% coverage complete, with enterprise private 5G networks live for 150 Fortune 500 clients in logistics and manufacturing. Midwest and Southeast accelerating from 65% to 85% by year-end, bolstered by $500 million in Rural Digital Opportunity Fund grants. International footprints via JVs in Europe and Latin America: 5G SA live in Mexico City and Madrid, contributing 8% to global capex but poised for 25% EBITDA margins through spectrum sharing with Telefónica.

Now, to capital expenditures: We deployed $2.7 billion this quarter, within our guided range, bringing nine-month total to $8.1 billion—a 12% increase YoY, but with improving efficiency as opex per site falls 8% due to automation and AI-driven predictive maintenance. Breakdown: $1.9 billion (70%) on 5G RAN and transport, including 8,500 new small cells and 100Gbps backhaul upgrades for mmWave in stadiums. $500 million (19%) on core and edge computing: Hyperscale edge nodes co-located with AWS Outposts for media transcoding. $300 million (11%) on spectrum integration and fiber deepens preparing for 3.45-3.55 GHz CBRS expansion.

Full-year capex guidance remains $11.5-12.5 billion, skewed toward the higher end as we front-load 5G SA to capture 2024's enterprise boom. This represents 18% of revenue, down from 22% in 2022, reflecting capex-to-revenue efficiency better than Vodafone's. Post-2025, we expect stabilization at 14-16% as 5G matures and we harvest returns from higher ARPU tiers (5G plans 15% premium, driving 2.5% blended ARPU growth).

These investments fuel a virtuous cycle: 5G driving 45% YoY growth in premium data plans and 30% in media bundle attachments, with churn at a record low 0.9%. We're positioning ahead of catalysts like FIFA World Cup streaming and private 5G for Hollywood virtual production. Risks include supply chain delays on Ericsson gear, but our diversified vendor strategy—40% Nokia, 35% Samsung, 25% Open RAN—mitigates this. Overall, this disciplined commitment de-risks our network for 10%+ annual revenue CAGR through the decade, with ROIC exceeding 12% by 2026. We are also improving network reliability through AI predictive maintenance.
